en: Preface to the *Huayan Nianfo Samādhi Treatise*:

The *Mahāyāna Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "All sentient beings are not called awakened because, from the very beginning, their thoughts have continued in succession without ever being separated from thought;
'thought' refers to non-awakening (*abodha*). A Buddha is awakening (*bodhi*). To recollect the Buddha is to [recollect] by means of awakening."

This means gathering that which is non-awakened. As for the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), it gathers the non-awakened through awakening, thereby entering the ocean of perfect enlightenment.
The *Avataṃsaka* contains all the samādhis of the Buddhas, yet among them, the *nien-fo samādhi* is the king of all samādhis;
nothing is greater than this, nothing is more supreme than this, and nothing is more vast than this. Know this!
The lay practitioner Gui has cultivated the *nien-fo* samādhi for over ten years and has further entered deeply into one gate of the ocean-like meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Recently, while passing through Zhenjiang, he presented me with his work, the *Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Nien-fo Samādhi*,
which encapsulates the vast number of characters in the *Śrīkṣetra* and *Zaobo* commentaries within five or six thousand words, thereby making the sub-commentaries clear and concise.
The combined treatises are not many, and this treatise is not few. Furthermore, at the time when Zao Bo composed the treatises, the entire "Chapter on the Vows" had not yet reached this land;

thus, it appeared as a distinct variation in other pure lands. Only when this chapter was fully revealed would the meaning finally be complete, for it was surely through the supernatural empowerment of Amitābha Buddha that he enabled the Layman [Zao Bo] to manifest it according to the needs of the occasion.

Is this not the preaching of the Dharma that extensively guides all classes of beings? I humbly maintain that for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and cultivate the Pure Land, the defiled blood of afflictions is transformed into the pure milk of the Dharma.
Through mindfulness of the Buddha, one attains samādhi—what is called "mindfulness returning to non-mindfulness."

It transforms fresh milk into curd. Within samādhi, one practices mindfulness of the Buddha with diligence—what is called "mindfulness through non-mindfulness"—thereby transforming the curd into cream. By means of the *nien-fo* (buddhānusmṛti) samādhi, one traverses all samādhis;
only then does one fully realize the *nien-fo* samādhi, which transforms the cream into butter. Through this *nien-fo* samādhi...
It encompasses immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable samādhis, gathering them all into the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (nien-fo san-mei).
It is both the remembrance and the Buddha; it is neither remembrance nor Buddha.

Its subtle and wondrous supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are inconceivable—it transforms matured ghee into clarified butter (*sarpis*), yet cannot transform milk into curds. Although one practices Buddha-remembrance...
One cannot attain the gates of samādhi; one cannot transform curd into ghee; one cannot, by means of the *nien-fo* (buddhānusmṛti) samādhi, encompass all unspeakable gates of samādhi;

one cannot transform ghee and curd into clarified butter (*sarpis*); and one cannot, through the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha alone, directly transcend the ten stages and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) to obtain the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and sit in realization of unsurpassed bodhi.

Indeed, while there is no distinction in the practice of *nien-fo* (recollection of the Buddha), there are varying depths of *samādhi*. The shallowness or depth of *samādhi* constitutes the distinctions within *nien-fo*.
From his youth, Bunchi delighted in the cultivation of Zen; it was only after the age of forty that he began to cultivate *nien-fo* concurrently.
In recent years, he has taken *nien-fo* as his Zen and Zen as his *nien-fo*, bringing both Zen and Pure Land together until the end of his life.

I have grown old. I venture to submit what I have seen to the Layman for verification, hoping that he will deign to instruct me. Written by the student Wang Wenzhi on the final day of the third month of spring in the year of Jiachen.
*Huayan Nianfo Sanmei Lun* (Treatise on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation According to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
Composed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Peng Jiqing:

A Discourse on the Dharma Gate of Buddha-Recitation. The various sūtras extensively praise this method. To summarize its essential principles, there are briefly two approaches: first, universal recollection (*pǔniàn*); second, focused recollection (*zhuānniàn*).
For instance, the *Sūtra on the Ocean of Marks of the Buddha* and the *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha* clarify only the method of universal recollection.

In sutras such as the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-tathāgata-sūtra*, the *Akṣobhya-buddha-sūtra*, and the *Amitāyus-sūtra*, the practice of exclusive recollection (*ekāgrasmṛti*) is specifically elucidated.
Now, in this *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the one and the many interpenetrate, the principal and the associates merge, the self and the other are identical, and it is both exclusive and universal.
Briefly stated, five meanings are set forth to unify the entire scripture: the Buddha-dharmakāya within a single thought-moment directly points to the self-nature of sentient beings.
1. The Gate of Recollecting the Buddha’s Merit: The Gate of Producing the Reward and Transformation Bodies of All Buddhas. 2. The Gate of Recollecting the Buddha’s Name:
The Gate of Accomplishing the Most Supreme Expedient Means. 3. The Gate of Recollecting Vairocana Buddha: The Gate of Instantaneous Entry into the Avataṃsaka Dharmadhātu. 4.
The Gate of Recollecting Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss: The Gate of Perfecting the Great Vows of Samantabhadra. A separate presentation of questions and answers follows.
It shatters all delusions and universally enables those who see and hear it to return together to the One Vehicle. This is what is meant:
the Buddha-dharmakāya pointed directly at the self-nature of sentient beings in a single thought-moment is our own inherent nature—tranquil, luminous, and pervading all lands and moments.
The Buddhas have nothing else to realize; they have realized nothing other than the self-nature of sentient beings. As it says:

The *Samantabhadracaryā-nirdeśa-parivarta* states: "A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should know their own mind: in every thought-moment, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not attain perfect enlightenment apart from this mind. As it is with one's own mind..."
The minds of all sentient beings are also like this. Within them all, the Tathāgata has attained equal and perfect enlightenment;

it is vast and pervasive, existing everywhere, never departing, never ceasing, and without rest. It is further said: there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
However, because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachments, they are unable to realize it. If they were to depart from...
When deluded conceptualization ceases, all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge will then manifest before one. (End of text. How does one depart from deluded conceptualization?
One must know that the inverted attachments of all sentient beings are entirely the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas. Why is this?
Because inverted attachments are eternally quiescent by their very nature. Entering into faith herein, the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is nowhere absent.
It is unmanifest, pure, and perfect, leaving no room for anything else within. Moment by moment there is no delusion; thought after thought there is nothing to grasp.
From this, one gives rise to practice, fully endowed with great compassion and ultimately possessing great loving-kindness. One takes nothing in the body and remains unattached to cultivation.

One abides nowhere within phenomena. Passing through the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage, one never departs from the present thought, wherein cause and effect are perfectly fulfilled.
Therefore it is said: "As soon as one gives rise to bodhicitta, one immediately achieves perfect enlightenment.

This is explained in detail in such passages as the "Chapter on the Merit of the Initial Resolve" in the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*. By recollecting the Buddha in this manner, one is able to see him in all places.
The body of the Tathāgata is like that described in the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance," where the World-Honored One emits ten billion rays of light from this trichiliocosm,
illuminating the ten directions throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space; therein Mañjuśrī speaks in verse,
instructing people to abandon all various views— such as existence and non-existence, unity and difference, arising and ceasing, and coming and going— pervading all things.
To contemplate the Tathāgata in all places is to enter into right faith in the Buddha. The "Chapter on Manifestation" also says:
"All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should not perceive the Tathāgata in a single dharma, a single thing, a single body, a single land, or a single sentient being;
rather, they should perceive the Tathāgata pervading all places, just as empty space pervades all form and non-form."
The sphere of form neither reaches nor does not reach. Why? Because space has no body. The body of the Tathāgata is likewise:
it pervades all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, and all lands.
Neither reaching nor not reaching. Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is no-body; yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests that body. It is further said:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of unobstructed and unhindered wisdom, knows all worldly realms;
this is the realm of the Tathāgata. He knows all realms of the three periods of time and all realms of all lands."
The realm of all phenomena; the realm of all sentient beings; the realm of non-differentiation of suchness; the realm of non-obstruction of the dharma-realm;
the realm of the limitlessness of the reality-limit; the realm of the measurelessness of space;
the realm that is no realm—this is the realm of the Tathāgata. Son of the Buddha, just as the realms of all worlds are immeasurable, so too is this realm.
The realm of the Tathāgata is likewise immeasurable. Just as the realms of all three periods of time are immeasurable, so too is the realm of the Tathāgata immeasurable.
Even as the realm of the non-realm is immeasurable, so too is the realm of the Tathāgata immeasurable.
Just as there is no objective realm (*viṣaya*) in any place whatsoever, so too is the realm of the Tathāgata; it does not exist anywhere.
(End of text. Why is this? Because the wisdom of one’s own mind is fundamentally without obstruction, and unobstructed wisdom is precisely the realm of the Tathāgata.
This is called "recollection of the Buddha as self-nature" (*svabhāva-buddha-smṛti*), and it is also called "recollection of the Buddha as self-nature."

Regarding mindfulness of the Buddha as self-nature (*svabhāva-buddhānusmṛti*): there is no Buddha external to the mindfulness that can be mindful of the Buddha. Regarding mindfulness of the Buddha as self-nature:

there is no Buddha external to the mindfulness that serves as the object of one's own mindfulness. If one does not enter this gate, the Buddha who is the object of mindfulness will ultimately not be the ultimate reality.
Because they do not recognize the intrinsic nature of the dharmakāya and mistakenly believe that it exists separately, when they enter this gate,
the merit of a single thought-moment surpasses empty space and is without limit.
Second, regarding the manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* Buddhas through the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha:
all Tathāgatas, equal in measure to the Dharma-realm, manifest various bodies, display inexhaustible adornments, and perform boundless Buddha-activities.

These are all essentially constituted by the wisdom of universal radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*). As stated in the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the Lord of the World": "Wisdom enters the three periods of time, being entirely equal. Its...
His body fills all worlds, and his voice universally accords with the lands of the ten directions.

It is like empty space, which contains all forms, yet makes no distinctions among any objects. (End of text) Because this wisdom is inconceivable and without limits, he is able to fully possess such power and function;
thus, while still on the level of an ordinary person, upon hearing the Dharma, he enters into the principle and attains [realization].

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). If one cannot rely on this wisdom to give rise to practice, cultivating and realizing it in its perfection, one will fall into the realm of the Śrāvaka vehicle of the two vehicles, and the great functions of the Buddhas will fail to manifest before them.
For this reason, the first six chapters of this sutra fully reveal the fruit-virtue (*phala-guṇa*) of the Tathāgata;
from the second assembly through the eighth assembly, comprising thirty-two chapters, they clarify the stages of progressive cultivation, leading all the way to...

Bodhi, in brief, does not transcend the six stages of cause and effect. To enable the practitioner to clarify and expand the realm of wisdom, to exhaust all gates of practice, and to adorn the Buddha-lands without clinging to a partial emptiness, there is the single chapter on Samantabhadra’s Samādhi within the first assembly.
This clearly reveals the entire body of the Buddha’s *Avataṃsaka*. The Sūtra explains how the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra enters the Samādhi of the Universal Body-Treasury of all Buddhas, Vairocana.
This samādhi relies upon the Dharma-realm; in accordance with its nature, it is all-pervasive.

Within the atoms of all lands, his universal body manifests, teaching all sentient beings without abandoning their worldly toil, extensively manifesting great functions as he preaches according to their needs.
In the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World," the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" is taught to demonstrate that all lands—whether pure or defiled—are solely the mind.
For those who can deeply penetrate the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows, there is nowhere that is not a Buddha-land and no time that is not a Buddha-activity.
This "Chapter on Samādhi" runs throughout the entire scripture; one may see this for oneself by examining the text. Upon reaching the youth Sudhana...

The son traveled extensively to consult various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). Yet, the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, the Householder Vimokṣa, and the Layman Vaiśravaṇa all attained liberation through the single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
As Meghaśrī said: "I have attained the power of decisive understanding and mastery;
the eye of faith is purified, the light of wisdom shines radiantly, and as I universally contemplate all spheres of experience, I am free from all obstructions and possess skillful means."
Observing with the all-pervading eye, clear and penetrating, and endowed with pure conduct, he proceeds to all lands throughout the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas.

He constantly keeps all Buddha-Tathāgatas in mind, upholds the true Dharma of all Buddhas, and always beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions. (End of text) By means of the power of my sovereign and decisive understanding, I...

"Going down" refers to the contemplation of the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*). "Proceeding to the ten directions" and so forth refers to the contemplation of the Reward-body and Transformation-body Buddhas (*saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*).

Following in accordance with the Dharma-body, the Reward and Transformation bodies arise; since the Dharma-body is immeasurable, the Reward and Transformation bodies it evokes are likewise immeasurable.
Therefore, the subsequent text says: "One sees one Buddha, two Buddhas, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, a hundred thousand Buddhas in the eastern direction."
...up to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-lands.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir (end of text).
This is called the Dharma-door of the Universal Vision of the Wisdom-Light Realm of All Buddhas. Buddhas have no separate realm; they possess only the light of wisdom.
Just as [the Buddha] performs buddha-work in accordance with sentient beings, so too is it for this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha.

Because they are fully endowed with faith and understanding, they are able to enter the wisdom of the Buddha; because they are fully endowed with contemplative practice, they are able to see the Buddha’s radiance and the radiance of wisdom.
This wisdom-radiance is not obtained from others; it is manifested solely by relying on conditions and causes. Furthermore, the subsequent text opens up the various great...

The Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of Mindfulness of the Buddha in Twenty-one Days: throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, and within every space as small as a single hair-tip, in every thought-moment a Buddha appears in the world, in every thought-moment a Buddha preaches the Dharma, and in every thought-moment a Buddha passes into parinirvāṇa.

This takes as its essence the boundless wisdom-practice of one's own mind, which inherently possesses the three bodies (trikāya). When this corresponds in a single thought-moment, it is called the "Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi" (Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha).
...obscured. Upon entering this gate of samādhi, one is able to universally encompass all gates of samādhi. Furthermore, as the Elder Vimukta said:
"I enter and emerge from the Tathāgata’s gate of liberation called 'Unimpeded Adornment.
Therein I see Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions. Those Tathāgatas do not come here to me, nor do I go to them. I...
If one wishes to see the Tathāgata Amitābha of the world Sukhāvatī, one shall see him immediately according to one's wish.

If I wish to see the Tathāgata Vajraprabhāsa of the world Candana, the Tathāgata Ratnaprabhāsa of the world Sugandha, the Tathāgata Ratnapadmaprabhāsa of the world Padma, the Tathāgata Śāntaprabha of the world Suvarṇa, or [the Tathāgata of] Su... [I shall see them immediately].
He saw all these [Buddhas] directly: Akṣobhya Tathāgata in the world Sukhāvatī; Siṃha Tathāgata in the world Supratiṣṭhita;
Candrabuddhi Tathāgata in the world Ādarśaprabhāsa; and Vairocana Tathāgata in the world Ratnasiṃhavicitra.
He realized that all Buddhas and his own mind were entirely like a dream. He knew all...
The Buddhas are like reflected images; one's own mind is like water. One knows that all the physical forms and characteristics of all Buddhas, as well as one's own mind, are entirely like illusions.
One knows that all Buddhas and one's own mind are entirely like echoes. Thus do I know, thus do I recollect:
all the Buddhas I behold arise solely from my own mind. (End of text) This is what is called "Unobstructed Adornment."
Liberation is to be free from all marks while yet manifesting all marks. Although it is like a dream and like an illusion, it does not destroy the various objects of dreams and illusions.

If one does not enter this dharma-gate of dreams and illusions, then one will be like Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others in the Jeta Grove, who do not perceive the realm of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power because their roots of goodness are insufficient.

Because they are identical. Furthermore, as Vessantara said: "When I opened the door of the Tathāgata’s stūpa containing the sandalwood throne, I attained a samādhi named 'The Inexhaustibility of the Buddha-seed.
Entering this samādhi, I beheld, in their proper sequence, all the Buddhas of this world, namely:
Kāśyapa Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, and Śi..."
The Buddhas Kāśyapa, Vipaśyin, Tiṣya, Puṣya, Anuttarajaya, and Anuttarapadma— taking these as their leaders—
they were able, in a single thought-moment, to see one hundred Buddhas, one thousand Buddhas, one hundred thousand Buddhas,
and even as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds. (End of text) This is the lineage of the Buddhas.
All [of these] arise from the vows and practices of Samantabhadra. Indeed, the vows and practices of Samantabhadra are all accomplished through the four inexhaustible phrases:

namely, "When the realm of empty space is exhausted, when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, when the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, and when the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted, my vow shall then be exhausted.
Yet, because the realm of empty space up to the afflictions are themselves inexhaustible, [my vow is likewise inexhaustible]. This is so.
Thus, the lineage of the Buddhas is inexhaustible. Therefore it is said: "I know that all Tathāgatas of the ten directions ultimately never enter parinirvāṇa.
This means that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation bodies) and *sambhogakāya* (reward bodies) of all Buddhas encompass all numerical categories, as explained in the "A-saṃkhyeya" chapter;
they exhaust all time, as explained in the "Tathāgata-āyus-pramāṇa" chapter; and they pervade all places, as explained in the "Bodhisattva-vihāra" chapter.

Thus it is said: "To thus recollect the Buddha is to realize the equality of the two limits, wherein arising and ceasing are one and the same, continuing without interruption throughout all future kalpas.
Third, regarding the accomplishment of the most supreme expedient through the names of the Buddha: for the Dharma-body is without trace; it is provisionally designated by means of names."
Thus, the Dharma-body is manifested, and its recompense and transformation bodies are boundless; by relying upon their names, these recompense and transformation bodies are fully encompassed.
As the "Verse Praise on Mount Sumeru" states: "It would be better to undergo the sufferings of hell than to receive immeasurable bliss while failing to hear the names of the Buddhas.
Therefore, in the past, throughout countless kalpas, one suffered and transmigrated within birth and death because one did not hear [the Buddha's name]."
Because of the name of the Buddha, merely hearing the name of the Buddha plants a supreme cause; how much more so for those who repeatedly maintain mindfulness of it!
As the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-pāramitā Sūtra* states: "One who wishes to enter the Samādhi of One Practice should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and not grasp at appearances.
Fixing the mind on a single Buddha, one should single-mindedly recite his name. Following the direction of that Buddha, one should sit upright and face toward him. Thus, one can..."
The continuous succession of thoughts regarding a single Buddha is precisely that within these thoughts one can perceive all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Why is this? Because the merit of one Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, and it is no different from the merit of immeasurable Buddhas.
(End of passage) The *Amitābha Sūtra* likewise takes the upholding of the Name as the primary cause for rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Therefore, we know that...
The merit of the names [of the Buddhas] is inconceivable. Furthermore, as stated in the "Verses of Praise" (Gāthā-stava) of the *Tuṣita* chapter:

"Taking the Buddha as one's object of focus, if one contemplates him with undistracted mindfulness, such a person shall behold the Buddhas; their number shall be equal to that of one's own thoughts. And as stated in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*):
If one constantly recollects the Buddha with an unmoving mind, then one will constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas.

If one constantly beholds immeasurable Buddhas, then one sees that the essence of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding. The preceding verse discussed the holding of the name, and thus spoke of "counting.

The subsequent [verse] encompasses both the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) to penetrate the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and thus speaks of "immeasurability. Nevertheless, while people know what it means to have a measurable count, they do not know how to transcend it.
The measure is its number; to know it is to know the name of number, yet not to know the name of that which transcends number.

Because one knows the name of that which transcends number, one contemplates throughout the day without ever contemplating. Because one knows the number that transcends measure, one contemplates a single Buddha and thereby universally encompasses all Buddhas.
As stated in the *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-parivarta*: "Just as I speak of 'self,' yet do not cling to it."
I do not cling to a self, nor to what belongs to a self. All Buddhas are likewise; they call themselves Buddhas, yet they do not cling to a self or to what belongs to a self.
(End of text. However, when first entering this gate, one must rely upon numerical counts.

One must establish a daily schedule, progressing from one to ten thousand, and from ten thousand to a hundred million. The mindfulness never leaves the Buddha, and the Buddha is no different from the mind, like the moon reflected in water.

Water and moon: the moon is not within the water, yet spring is not outside the branches. Thus, when one recollects the Buddha, the name is itself the Dharma-body, because the nature of the name cannot be apprehended;
the Dharma-body is itself the name, because the Dharma-body pervades all things.
It is likewise that the recompense and transformation bodies are not different from names, and names are not different from the recompense and transformation bodies.
Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgata," it is said that the name of a single Tathāgata is equal to the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space;

according to the minds of sentient beings, they each perceive and see it differently. Thus, one knows that whatever names exist in the world are themselves the names of the Buddha. To cite any one of them—
As for "names," there is no name among all the worlds that is not subsumed herein.

Furthermore, as in the Vairocana Chapter, where the various Buddhas of antiquity are cited differently, yet each is collectively designated by the name Vairocana—because all Buddhas possess the body of the Vairocana-treasury and because they do not differ across past and present—one recollects the Buddha in this manner; by holding the name of a single Buddha, one fully encompasses them all.
The Dharma-realm. The name of the entire Dharma-realm encompasses the whole Dharma-realm; it is not of the past, not of the present, and not of the future.

Nor does it belong to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below—the ten directions and the three periods of time. In this very thought-moment, without remainder and without passing through even a single kṣaṇa, one has already completed the attainment of Buddhahood.

Regarding the fourfold mindfulness of Vairocana Buddha’s immediate entry into the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is as expressed in the various verses spoken by the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as the devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts, in the "Chapter on the Exquisite Array of the World Lord. Each of these arises from their own realized dharma-gates;

through the fruit-ground of the Tathāgata, they inspire faith and understanding in others, causing them to enter the samādhi of Buddha-recollection. From this point onward, the teaching proceeds as follows:

In the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs," as well as in the chapters on the Ten Faiths, the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Dedications, great Bodhisattvas from the ten directions and various world-rulers each speak verses in praise of the Buddha.
Furthermore, in every stage of the "Ten Grounds" chapter, it is invariably stated that one must not depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
Thus, we know that although the various stages and ranks differ, none of them fail to rely upon these [threefold mindfulnesses].
The practice of *buddhānusmṛti* (recollection of the Buddha) is its fundamental practice. The Way of all Buddhas is the same; by invoking one Vairocana, nothing is left uncomprised.
Thus, it is said in the "Single Gate" of the *Samantabhadra-daśapraṇidhāna* that one constantly follows the Buddha’s learning:

"In this Sahā world, the Tathāgata Vairocana, from his first aspiration for enlightenment, practiced with diligence without retreating, offering unspeakably unspeakable numbers of his own bodies and lives..."
From practicing generosity up until attaining great Bodhi and entering Nirvana—I shall follow and learn all such deeds as these.

(End of text) Because the practices performed by my Original Teacher while on the path of causes were vast, boundless, and inconceivable, the retributive manifestations he elicited are likewise vast, boundless, and inconceivable.
If a practitioner can truly and resolutely believe and understand this, [they shall attain the same].
Knowing that all Buddhas do not depart from their own nature, one gives rise to a courageous mind and a mind of responsibility;
this is no different from the time when one’s original teacher first resolved to attain enlightenment. Furthermore, as the night goddess Silent Ocean-Voice said:
"I have attained the liberation of 'producing vast joy and adornment in every thought-moment,' by which I am able to enter ten times unspeakably unspeakable [realms]."
Within oceans of the establishment of dharma-realms, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, I beheld all those oceans of the establishment of dharma-realms.
Within every single atom of all those buddha-fields, there were ten times the number of buddha-lands as there are atoms in an unspeakably unspeakable number of buddha-fields.
In each of those buddha-lands, Vairocana was seated upon the path of enlightenment.
In every moment of thought, he attains perfect enlightenment and manifests various spiritual transformations. Each of these manifested transformations pervades the entire ocean of all dharma-realms.

Thus, the Night Goddess Tree-Blossom-Open has entered the liberation door of "Giving Birth to the Radiance of Vast Great Joy," and she clearly perceives, in their entirety, the oceans of practices cultivated by Vairocana in the past.
The liberation door of the divine power of Sovereignty over Birth through the Perfection of Sublime Virtue:
entering the immeasurable ocean of Vairocana’s births, one also beholds the Tathāgata within every single atom of all worlds, amidst infinite Buddha-fields.
The manifestation of taking birth is constant and uninterrupted. (End of text. Thus, to contemplate Vairocana is to contemplate this Buddha; this Buddha is itself contemplation.
Throughout the entirety of the void of the ten directions, even down to the space occupied by a needle-point or a mustard seed, there is not a single thing that is not the Dharma-realm of Vairocana.
This is called "contemplating the Buddha of the Dharma-realm," and it is also called "universally contemplating all Buddhas. For this reason:
When the youth Sudhana first visited Meghashri, he immediately heard the teaching on the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Finally, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva spoke for him the verses praising the supreme merits of the Tathagata to instruct him in faith and understanding; yet, from beginning to end, this did not depart from the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Within the Dharmadhatu, there are ultimately no two truths. The verse says: "Or one may see this realm as wondrous beyond compare... [The Buddha...]
Adorned and purified over immeasurable eons, the most supreme Honored One, Vairocana, attained awakening and realized *bodhi* therein.
Some see the Buddha Amitāyus, surrounded by Avalokiteśvara and others, all of whom abide in the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), filling all worlds throughout the ten directions.
It is further said: some see Śākyamuni having already attained the Way of the Buddha. Not long ago...
In inconceivable kalpas, one may see him now beginning his career as a bodhisattva, benefiting all sentient beings throughout the ten directions;

or one may see the Tathāgata Amitāyus bestowing the prediction of supreme enlightenment upon various bodhisattvas, so that they become unsurpassed Great Teachers and succeed him in dwelling within the Land of Peace and Bliss.
(End of text) From this we know that the Dharmadhātu of all Buddhas is universally encompassing and universally interfused; Amitābha is entirely...
The essence of Vairocana’s Sukhāvatī is not separate from the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha), yet it appears differently according to the minds of sentient beings;
however, because the Buddha is fundamentally and eternally unmoving, the final fascicle concludes with the dedication of merit toward Sukhāvatī, as is fully explained in the subsequent text.
Regarding the five recollections of Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the fulfillment of the Great Vows of Samantabhadra, the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* states:
"One who wishes to accomplish the gateway to the Tathāgata’s merits should cultivate ten kinds of vast practices and vows.
First, prostrating to all Buddhas; second, praising the Tathāgatas; third, extensively cultivating offerings; fourth, repenting..."
5. Repenting of karmic obstructions; 6. Rejoicing in merit; 7. Requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; 8.
Requesting the Buddhas to remain in the world; 9. Constantly following and learning from the Buddhas; 10. Universally dedicating all merits.
If one upholds, recites, and studies this King of Vows, at the time of death, one will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. (End of text)
This sutra exclusively reveals the realm of Vairocana; why, then, should one take Sukhāvatī as its ultimate goal?
It is because the name Amitābha means "Immeasurable Light," and Vairocana is translated here as "Universal Radiance"; since they are of one and the same essence, [the two are identical].
Because it is neither past nor future; for within a single essence, there is likewise no obstruction to its being past or future.
As stated in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*: "When sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds may become timid and weak.

Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they cannot constantly encounter the Buddhas to personally receive their teachings and make offerings. For those whose resolve might thus regress, one should know that..."

There is a superior expedient for protecting and sustaining one’s faith: namely, to single-mindedly recollect Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, dedicate all roots of goodness cultivated toward the aspiration to be born in that world, and thereby attain rebirth there.
Because one constantly beholds the Buddha, there shall never be any falling back. (End of text) For the Reward Land of Vairocana has no connection with those of the Two Vehicles or ordinary beings.

In contrast, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), there are nine grades of rebirth; yet like myriad streams rushing toward a single ocean, once one attains birth there, one cuts across the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) horizontally.
When compared to this Sahā world, the difference between their excellence and inferiority is vast and distinct, as extensively clarified in various sutras, which I shall not record here in full.
However, what other sutras point to varies: some speak of ten recitations, some of one day up to seven days, and some of contemplating the sixteen-foot [Buddha]. Now...
Even extending to sixty trillion nayutas of *gaṅgā*-sands of *yojanas*, such measurements ultimately do not escape the realm of numerical calculation;

they cannot compare to the universal contemplation in a single thought-moment of this sutra, which vertically exhausts the three periods of time and horizontally spans the ten directions of empty space.

At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one transcends all numerical measures. All such causes of purity are most exceptionally sublime, because Amitābha Buddha, by means of his forty-eight [vows]...
May I universally embrace all sentient beings, so that this King of Vows merges with the body of space, without the slightest interval.
Therefore, without shifting time or changing place, may I be born spontaneously, returning to what was originally attained. As the subsequent text says:
"Having arrived, one immediately sees Amitābha Buddha, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and..."
Surrounded by Maitreya Bodhisattva and others (end of text). Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra do not depart from this place yet manifest in other regions;
they appear in every thought-moment according to the minds of sentient beings. Thus, one should know that Amitābha Buddha resides in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

One should constantly turn this sutra, burning with vigor without interruption. Furthermore, regarding this Dharma-gate, were it not for the observation of wondrous wisdom, there would be no way to clarify the pure cause inherent within my own mind;
thus, Mañjuśrī is placed first. Were it not for the adornment of great vows, there would be no way to perfect the pure fruit inherent within my own mind;
thus, Samantabhadra follows next. As for Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya, the former succeeds [Samantabhadra] because he is next in line to succeed [the Buddha].
Maitreya shall first succeed Śākyamuni; these two sages will assemble together to testify that the Land of Bliss and the Flower Treasury Realm (Huazang) are fundamentally one and not two.

Maitreya, through his contemplation of the ten directions as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), realizes that the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous and enters the state of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
this is the primary cause for this Pure Land. Avalokiteśvara, by means of the effortless, wondrous power of illusory-like auditory permeation (*śruta-vāsanā*), enters universally into all realms.
The Land. One achieves enlightenment; this is the ultimate fruit of this Pure Land. As the subsequent text states:
"That person sees themselves born within a lotus flower and receives a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha.

Having received this prediction, after the passage of countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, by the power of wisdom, they bring benefit to sentient beings according to their minds. Before long, they shall sit upon the seat of enlightenment."
He ascended the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), subdued the armies of Māra, attained equal and perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma.
He was able to cause sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field to resolve upon Bodhicitta;

according to their faculties and natures, he taught and matured them, continuing until the end of the ocean-like kalpas of the future, extensively benefiting all sentient beings. (End of text) The entirety of the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra] is contained herein.
Conclusion: All wise people should certainly believe and enter [this path]. A single moment of negligence leads to endless saṃsāra; alas, what suffering! Someone may ask:
"Regarding the five gates mentioned above, should one enter through a single gate, or should one enter all five gates? Answer: As stated above...
With sharp faculties and wisdom, one realizes the self-nature of Amitābha and fully manifests the Pure Land of Mind-Only. By invoking the single Dharma-body, nothing is not encompassed.

Nevertheless, while principle is realized suddenly, practice must be eliminated gradually. Thus, according to the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, those at the initial stage of the Ten Abodes are identical to all Buddhas;

yet, as they progress through the five stages of cultivation, there remains a direction toward which they move until the level of Sublime Enlightenment is reached. This constitutes the sequence of stages.

It is exactly so. From the beginning to the end of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), by the power of great vows, one perceives many hundreds, many thousands, and even hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of Buddhas within a single moment of thought. The lands where these Buddhas reside are all ranked according to the specific Buddhas perceived therein.
Although practitioners in this land may be able to subdue their afflictions and attain awakening, they have not yet realized the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda*).
If one does not rely on the power of the Buddha, it will be difficult to perfect one's merit and practice even after escaping future existence;

one must instead await rebirth in the Land of Bliss, where one may personally receive the prediction of enlightenment, purify all residual habits, and become a sovereign of fulfilled vows—this constitutes the wondrously adorned path that transcends all other gates.

Should one have a coarse glimpse of that which transcends [the mundane] yet fail to exhaust all doubts, one must especially focus single-mindedly on holding the Name, exerting oneself with diligence and making vows like a child yearning for its mother, taking the end of life as the limit.
Furthermore, by cultivating through both teaching and contemplation (*śikṣā*), one assists in the awakening of supreme wisdom;

when response and resonance meet in the Way, merit will not be spent in vain. This is entirely dependent upon a single thought-moment to encompass all gateways; what is most precious is the severing of worldly interests.
One Source. One must strictly avoid turning back or shifting one's perspective.
He asked again: "If you wish to expound the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-Recitation, why do you not take the various Pure Land sutras as your guide, but instead insist upon the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*?
To argue for the cause based on the fruit may well prove difficult to reconcile. He replied: "Have you not read the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*?"

In the introductory section of the sutra, the practices and vows of Samantabhadra are first described to encourage practitioners; it is stated that those reborn in the three grades all "give rise to the bodhicitta.

It concludes by declaring that one who does not realize the Buddha’s wisdom—the inconceivable wisdom, the incomparable wisdom, the peerless and supreme wisdom—even if they cultivate meritorious deeds, will still fall back into birth from a womb. Thus, if one truly wishes to sit [in the lotus posture...]

Upon the precious lotus flower, one ascends to the stage of non-retrogression; this must necessarily rely upon the wisdom of Mañjuśrī and establish the vows of Samantabhadra, turning the mind toward rebirth there.

This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is precisely the teaching for that purpose. As for those who attain the highest grade of the highest birth according to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, they must recite and study the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
Regarding what is called "Mahāyāna Vaipulya," none is more supreme than the *Avataṃsaka*.
First: Since cause and effect are without discrepancy, what circuitousness could there be?
Furthermore, it was asked: "The Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka contains a layering of profound meanings, with immeasurable sūtras serving as its retinue."
How is it that the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha alone can universally encompass all? Answer: It is exactly as you have said; the teaching points toward the vast and profound.
However, for those at the initial stage of entering the Way, there is a specific expedient means: by entering this one gate, one is able to penetrate everywhere throughout the boundless Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within a single pore of Samantabhadra, the youth Sudhana passed through unspeakably unspeakable [aeons].
It is said that throughout world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field, for all kalpas of the future, one reaches every corner of the boundless ocean of lands in every thought-moment.

This person who practices the recollection of the Buddha is likewise so, because a single thought is fundamentally immeasurable. Furthermore, Dushun’s *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* specifically establishes three gates:
first, the Gate of True Emptiness, which eliminates deluded sentiments to reveal the principle; this is precisely the aforementioned practice of recollecting the Buddha.

The first is the gate of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā* and *dharma*), which integrates principle and phenomena to manifest function; this is precisely the aforementioned merit of recollecting the Buddha.
The third is the gate of universal inclusion, which encompasses all phenomena to reveal the source; this is precisely the aforementioned names of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the *Qingliang shu* (Commentary on the Pure and Cool) divides the four dharma-realms as follows: First, when one recollects the Buddha with the mind, unmixed with other activities, one enters the phenomenal dharma-realm (*shifa jie*).
When both mind and Buddha are simultaneously extinguished, and the single truth stands alone in liberation, one enters the noumenal dharma-realm (*lifafa jie*).

When the mind is the Buddha and the great functions are fully manifested, one enters the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomenon and noumenon (*lishi wuai fajie*). When there is neither Buddha nor mind, and the divine mystery is unfathomable, one enters... [the dharma-realm of the perfect interpenetration of all phenomena].
The Dharma-realm of non-obstruction in all phenomena is known as the single thought-moment gate of mindfulness; there is no dharma that it does not encompass.
Therefore, this sutra takes Vairocana as its guide and Sukhāvatī as its destination. Having beheld Amitābha, one does not depart from the Flower Treasury World (Huazang);
household treasures are fully present and its power and function are boundless. Without entering this gate, one will ultimately never reach the final goal.
He asked again: "The *Fangshan lun* asserts that the pure lands of other directions are provisional and not ultimate. According to the discussion presented here, how should this be reconciled?

He replied: "The teachings distinguish four lands: first, the land of constant quiescent light (*nitya-prabhāsa-dharmatā-kāya*), which is the dwelling place of the Buddha of fruition; second, the land of true retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*)."
The *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas dwell in the Land of Ultimate Purity (*suddhāvāsa-bhūmi*). The Two Vehicles dwell in the Land of Residual Existence (*traidhātuka-śeṣa-bhūmi*).

The Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-bhūmi*) is where ordinary beings and sages intermingle; it is either defiled or pure. Those who practice in this land, through the power of single-minded mindfulness, cultivate various merits and dedicate them toward the West.

While their afflictions and karma are not yet severed, they are born into the Land of Common Residence. As their longing for transcendence and aversion to the mundane grow keen, their coarse outflows gradually diminish, and they hear the Dharma.

They advance and are born in the lands of remaining existence (*sopadhiśeṣa*). If one cultivates the Perfect Teaching as the cause, deeply penetrating the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and dedicates [the merit] through the practices and vows of Samantabhadra toward rebirth, one will then attain the land of true recompense (*vipākabhūmi*) and personally receive the Buddha’s prediction, partially realizing the land of tranquil light (*prabhāsvaraloka*).

Therefore, for those who abide in the provisional vehicles, everything is provisional—like the illusory city in the *Lotus Sūtra*—for it does not exist outside of one's own mind. Thus it is clarified.
As for the true aspect (*dharmatā*), everything is real. This is because this sutra’s *Sukhāvatī-vyūha* is entirely complete within the *Avataṃsaka*.

When Fangshan composed his commentary, the final fascicle of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* (the *Fangguang da zhuangyan jing*) had not yet reached this region; consequently, he inadvertently gave rise to distinctions regarding the single gate of the Pure Land.
Yet this contradicts the scriptural texts. One must understand that from the True arises the illusory, yet the illusory is entirely the True;

birth and extinction are both transcended, self and other are non-dual, and in a single thought-moment there is perfect integration, universally pervading the Dharma-realm—only then does it constitute the definitive meaning of the Middle Way of the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, Fāngshān’s urgent exhortation lies solely in the realization of perfect enlightenment at the very first moment of the Ten Abidings. However...

Judging according to the teachings, this is correct and unchanging. Why? Because within the stage of Perfect Faith, the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted, as well as the "dust-like" afflictions;
one then enters the stage of Perfect Abiding, where ignorance is suddenly shattered and the patience of non-arising is realized, equaling the first bhūmi of the Distinct Teaching.
If one relies on one's own power, it is like those common folk who suddenly aspire to the precious throne, claiming they have been Buddhas from the beginning and need not traverse the stages.
Yet, even this depends upon skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) before realization can finally be achieved.

How does this compare to what is taught in the final fascicle of the *Pratideśanā* (Vows and Practices), which states that by means of profound faith, one recites the Ten Great Vow-Kings and, in a single kṣaṇa, is reborn in Sukhāvatī to dwell in non-retrogression?

To turn back from the stage of ordinary beings and, having newly given rise to faith, to leap across directly and enter the ultimate, sudden, peerless, and incomparable [Dharma]—this is a rare encounter with the complete scripture;
the conditions for this are no small matter. The pearl within one's robes remains as before, yet to labor as a hired hand is but toil in vain.
I respectfully exhort those of noble character to unite in heart and receive it with faith.

He asked again: "The Sui monk Linggan practiced the visualization of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang guan*). At the time of his death, he saw a vast expanse of water filling everywhere, and he sat upon a flower as large as a chariot wheel.
He was able to proceed directly to the Flower Treasury World; why then would he need to further behold Amitābha? He replied:
"In the Flower Treasury World, there are ten times an unspeakable number of fragrant water seas, as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields."
World-systems as numerous as atoms abide [within these realms]. Within each world-system, there are further worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is also among them. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states:
"If one’s flying mind is endowed with both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will naturally open and one shall see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all pure [lands]."

As for rebirth in accordance with one's vows in the land of the Buddha: whether the spirit-stem (linggan) currently born here is in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, or in some other pure land, remains unknown.
Nevertheless, to behold Amitābha is itself to proceed directly toward the Flower Treasury World (Huazang).
In the past there was Śāriputra; in the later period, Nāgārjuna. Following such a precedent, a thousand sages have traveled the same path.
To disregard the Buddha’s injunctions and become exhausted on many divergent paths is what is called being pitiable. To further illustrate this with a recent example:

Dao-yin of the thatched hermitage in Mingzhou during the Song dynasty cultivated the contemplation of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching. Later, he presided over Yanqing Monastery. On the fourth month of the third year of the Qiandao era—

On the seventeenth day, he addressed his followers, saying: "The world of Avataṃsaka is profoundly transparent and luminously serene; it perfectly accords with my heart's desire. Now I am about to depart.

He then commanded that the *Maitreya Amitābha Praise* he had composed be recited: "The boundless ocean of lands contains the void within its waves; The ocean and the void are entirely the Lotus Palace.
The Lotus Palace pervades everywhere throughout the ocean of the void; Within this void-ocean, the countenance of Amitābha alone is revealed."
Amitābha Buddha is neither born nor extinguished; like the moon in water, he is difficult to grasp and difficult to seize. This body is utterly beyond words and conceptualization;
such is its resonance and such is its teaching. I and Amitābha are fundamentally non-dual; it is through the latent arising of deluded cognition that they suddenly appear as distinct.
From this day forth, I shall sweep away all dust of emptiness and existence, so that father and son may naturally meet face to face. I vow to cultivate the three blessings.

Diligently practice the six recollections. Let the actions of body, speech, and mind be free from flaw or blemish. "I now recite the name of Amitābha; until I behold Amitābha, I shall never grow weary.

Having finished this praise, he followed the assembly in chanting the Buddha’s name several hundred times. Reciting the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* up to the section on the highest grade of the highest birth, he then withdrew his thoughts and passed away while sitting upright.
Are the Pure Land (*Sukhāvatī*) and the Flower Adornment (*Avataṃsaka*) the same or different? All people of wisdom must urgently apply themselves to this.
The Eye.
This treatise was composed in the twelfth month of winter in the forty-eighth year of the Qianlong era. Once completed, Mr. Wang Dashi evaluated it, saying:
"This is the primary cause for the Pure Land; it is the authentic faith of the *Avataṃsaka*. He further remarked: "The five recollections..."
"Mindfulness. A single thought is no-thought. The following spring, he passed through Dantu. Prince Wuying saw him and praised his talent, composing a preface for him.
Dashen marveled at this as something truly extraordinary. Shortly thereafter, he performed the funeral rites for his late father, the Honorable Shangshu.
After the burial, he lived in seclusion within a monastic quarters, where he read and studied the Great Sūtras.
He engaged in mutual inquiry and verification with his friend from beyond the secular world, Xingzong Weiran, and occasionally made revisions and improvements to this treatise.

Several years later, upon returning from Qiantang, he once again closed himself off in the Wensheng Pavilion to cultivate the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation. During the long summer of profound stillness, he brought forth the previous draft once more.
I have carefully collated and revised this once more and recorded it as this edition. Outside the Fangshan collection of Xianshou, it need not be considered a separate tradition;
yet were one to encounter the Elder of Yunqi, he would surely look upon it and smile.

At the end of the waning moon of the sixth month in the fifty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, Ji Qing recorded this *Treatise on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation According to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. (End.)
